newsitem.title: USA: Avocet mulls raising tungsten production.
newsitem.headline: Avocet mulls raising tungsten production.

text.p: Avocet Mining may hike output next year because a huge supply shortage is expected to hit the market.

Robert Bunting, president of Avocet Tungsten Inc, the U.S. subsidiary of Avocet Mining, said preparations were underway to restart the company's majority-owned Malaga mine in Peru probably during the next few months.
Avocet is collectively the Western world's biggest tungsten producer.
Both of Avocet's majority-owned Peruvian mines -- the other is Regina -- stopped production in the middle of this year due to low tungsten prices.
"Regina is only producing from tailings," Bunting said. "We need to spend time and money to get the ore body to produce efficiently. At this point it is not clear how we will go with Regina."
Avocet is also considering adding another shift at Beralt, the company's Portuguese mine. Beralt has been restricted to one shift.
Avocet's wholly-owned Pine Creek ammonium paratungstate (APT) plant in California, relies to some extent on Peruvian tungsten concentrates to keep operating.
The nearby Pine Creek mine, half-owned by Avocet, has been idled for six years, but could be restarted within six months, Bunting said.

This year Avocet expected to produce 1,200 tonnes of contained tungsten metal from its worldwide operations, down from about 1,500 tonnes in 1995, Bunting said. At full production, Avocet could produce 3,300 tonnes.
The tungsten primary metal market will be in balance at the end of this year, helped by surplus free-market stocks to plug a 11,000-tonne supply gap.
Bunting said next year's gap will be 14,000 tonnes at current production and consumption levels. Only fresh production or sales from official stockpiles can bridge the gap, he added.
Producers met in China recently and agreed to lobby national stockpiles to think twice about sales.
